title: Teaching himself bass on his brother Johnny's instrument
summary: Garland went from guitar and mandolin to bass, sneaking his brother's bass until Johnny tested him on chords and taught him the changes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Okay. Could you tell us a little bit about the early -- about your early days. Were your parents in music, Tootie?
Yeah. Want me to tell you how it started out?

I first started with guitar. Then, I didn't care so much about the guitar. I jumped into it. My brother played mandolin, you know, and I finally picked up the mandolin and tried to play it, and it looked like I got to play the mandolin pretty fair. And I stayed on the mandolin for a while. Then I got crazy about bass.

My brother had a bass. He bought a bass from Sam Nicholson. And he used to tell me to never touch this bass. I'd say, 'Don't worry, Johnny. I ain't going to mess with the bass.' He said, 'You'd better not.' I said, okay, brother. So one day I looked up at that bass, you know, and I said, 'I believe I can play this bass.' I went and got the bass, and I started to messing around with it, and my grandmother said to me, 'Put that bass down. You know your brother don't want you to play that bass.' I said, 'Please let me play it a little bit. He'll never know. I ain't going to hurt it.' 'No, no. You might break the bass.' I said, 'I can't break it.' She said, 'Go ahead, but be very careful.' So I kept playing. I didn't know what I was doing, but I imagined I was playing. So finally, that evening, when he come home, I said, 'Johnny, I think I can play this bass.' 'You think you can play it?' I said, 'Yeah.' 'You been messing around with the bass?' I said, 'No, no, no. But I

just think I can play it." He said, "I'm going to see." So he went and got the guitar. He got the guitar, and the first thing, he started to make a few chords. He played a C, you know. So he says to me, "Let me see what you can do. You say you can play the bass." So I grabbed the bass, and the first thing I hit was F.
He said, "Now, what's the next chord you're going to make?" I made a B-flat, you know. Cross the fingerboard, from B-flat to F to C.
I didn't know what to do after that F and B-flat, you know.

And he said, "Now, just go right straight across there now, on that A string." And I hit the A-string, and it went, whoomp. He said, "You know what you're making?" I said, "No." He said, "That's C." So I said, "Oh, that's C, huh?" So I made C, F and B-flat. So he says, "I'll tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to show you a few chords on this bass and I want you to practice. When I come back this evening, I want to find out how much you learned. Will you do that?" I said, "Sure. I can do it." And I done it, too. I really played an F and B-flat pretty fair. The C and G, oh, I was it there. So when he come in -- you know,
He got the guitar and he played a little waltz. He hummed it, singing it, you know, playing it. It was in C, you know.
Uh-huh. And he'd tell me 'One D, two beats'.

And I played it. And he says, 'Now, you hit this G, you hit your C, then you hit your F.' So I done that. He said, 'That's pretty good.' So that's how I started out. And I kept on, kept on, until I could play, learn the changes in B-flat and F.
